objective: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to use correct subject-verb agreement in simple sentences in the context of discussing filmmakers and cinema.
materials: - Introduction to Academic Writing (3rd ed.), Chapter 1: Paragraph Format, pp10-13

stages.stage_aim: To activate learners' interest in George Lucas and cinema, and to raise awareness of typical Thai L1 subject-verb agreement errors
stages.procedure:
- Display a splash image of George Lucas on the IWB. Elicit what students know about him and his films. Build a word cloud on the board.
- Present 6 sentences about George Lucas containing typical Thai L1 subject-verb agreement errors. Students work in pairs to discuss what is wrong.
- Auto-animate the corrections to reveal the correct forms. Elicit why each correction was needed, but do not explain the rules yet.

stages.stage_aim: To diagnose learners' ability to identify and correct subject-verb agreement errors across five key trouble spots before explicit teaching
stages.procedure:
- Distribute a bespoke 8-sentence error-correction handout. All sentences are about George Lucas and cinema.
- Students work individually to find and correct one subject-verb agreement error in each sentence.
- Monitor closely and note which error types cause the most difficulty. Do not reveal answers yet.

stages.stage_aim: To draw out the five key rules of subject-verb agreement through guided analysis of model sentences from the George Lucas text, targeting only the problem areas observed in the diagnostic test
stages.procedure:
- Return to the diagnostic test items. Use show of hands to gauge which items students found hardest.
- Display the George Lucas model text from p10 on the IWB. Extract marker sentences that illustrate each tricky rule (e.g., "One new technology was a special computer-assisted camera crane").
- Elicit the generalisation for each rule before confirming:
  1. Ignore prepositional phrases between subject and verb.
  2. In 'There + be' sentences, the subject follows be — look ahead.
  3. Each, one, neither, either are always singular.
  4. Both, several, many are always plural.
  5. Some, all, most, a lot, none can be either — check the noun in the prepositional phrase.
- Board the five rules with textbook examples (pp12-13). Students copy into notebooks.

stages.stage_aim: To apply the five subject-verb agreement rules in controlled and freer practice contexts from the textbook
stages.procedure:
- Part A: Students complete Practice 3 Part A (items 1–11, p13) individually, choosing the correct verb form. Pair check. Whole-class feedback on the IWB.
- Part B: Students find and correct the six subject-verb agreement errors in the 'Young Golf Stars' paragraph (Practice 3 Part B, p14). Pairs compare. Reveal answers using the answer key on the IWB.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the five agreement rules and confirm that learners can produce accurate sentences independently
stages.procedure:
- Quick-fire oral drill: teacher says a subject phrase, students respond chorally with the correct verb form (e.g., 'Each of the students' → 'has').
- Students write two original sentences about a favourite film or filmmaker, each using a different agreement rule. Volunteers share on the board.
- Recap the five rules from the board. Answer any remaining questions.
